bug_description.original: Heap-buffer-overflow in load_protocols_file_fd OSS-Fuzz report: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=426164365 ``` Crash type: Heap-buffer-overflow READ 2 Crash state: load_protocols_file_fd fuzz_filecfg_protocols.c ```
bug_description.normalized: The staged `fuzz_filecfg_protocols` testcase is treated as a newline-delimited protocols file and also seeds the fuzz malloc wrapper with `size == 2924`, enabling deterministic allocation failures. On the crashing line, `load_protocols_file_fd` admits a non-comment rule containing `@<unknown protocol>` plus a `tcp:` attribute and passes it to `ndpi_handle_rule`. Because the protocol name after `@` is unknown, `ndpi_handle_rule` takes the custom-protocol path and sets `proto_id = ndpi_str->num_supported_protocols`, then calls `ndpi_set_proto_defaults` to ensure `proto_defaults[proto_id]` exists. When that `ndpi_realloc` fails, `ndpi_set_proto_defaults` returns early without updating `ndpi_str->proto_defaults` or `proto_defaults_num_allocated`, but the caller still forms `def = &ndpi_str->proto_defaults[proto_id]`. The later `tcp:` handling loop dereferences `def->tcp_default_ports[j].port_low`; AddressSanitizer shows that read landing 56 bytes past the old 65536-byte heap region, which is consistent with `proto_id` being at the old allocation limit when the unchecked alias is formed.

source.description: First project-side materialization of vulnerability-relevant attacker input: `fgets` reads a line from the staged in-memory protocols file into mutable heap buffer `buffer`, creating the rule string later parsed into the crashing custom-protocol definition.
source.value_from: The staged 2924-byte `poc` is exposed to project code through `fmemopen`. On the crashing iteration this read yields a non-comment rule line that contains an `@` suffix naming an unknown protocol and a later `tcp:` element, which is the minimum witnessed structure needed to reach the out-of-bounds `def->tcp_default_ports` access.

relation.description: Source identity relation for the vulnerability-relevant value.

root_cause.description: After `ndpi_set_proto_defaults` can return early on growth failure, `ndpi_handle_rule` still aliases `def` to `proto_defaults[proto_id]` without checking that the table was successfully expanded. In the witnessed path `proto_id` is already equal to the old allocation bound, so this statement creates an out-of-bounds pointer.
root_cause.note: The fix changes `ndpi_set_proto_defaults` to return an error and adds `if(ret != 0) return(-3);` before this assignment, which directly restores the missing failure check.

sink.description: Final crashing read. The `tcp:` attribute path walks `def->tcp_default_ports`, but `def` already points past the unchanged 512-entry `proto_defaults` heap array, so reading `port_low` dereferences out-of-bounds memory.
sink.note: AddressSanitizer reports `READ of size 2` at this line on address `0x531000024838`, which is 56 bytes past heap region `[0x531000014800,0x531000024800)` allocated for the older `proto_defaults` array.

parser_admitted.description: The staged protocols-file witness reaches the accepted continuation for a non-empty, non-comment rule line, which is the sample-specific loader gate before protocol-rule parsing begins.

tainted_value_origin.description: This lookup converts the attacker-controlled protocol suffix extracted from the admitted rule into the vulnerability-relevant `unknown protocol` state. That state is what forces the later custom-protocol allocation path instead of reusing an existing in-bounds default entry.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: The crashing rule's text after `@` does not match any built-in protocol name, so `ndpi_get_proto_by_name` returns `NDPI_PROTOCOL_UNKNOWN` and `def` stays `NULL`.
tainted_value_origin.note: Without this `unknown protocol` result, the code would set `def = &ndpi_str->proto_defaults[subprotocol_id]` and would not execute the failing custom-protocol growth path.

fine_trace.note: The harness seeds nDPI's malloc wrapper with the testcase size `2924`, so later `ndpi_malloc` and `ndpi_realloc` calls can deterministically return `NULL` on this run. This is the witnessed control precondition for the failed growth path fixed by the patch.
Source. `fgets` copies the next attacker-controlled line from the in-memory protocols file into heap buffer `buffer`, producing the mutable rule string parsed on the crashing iteration.
The materialized line from step 1 survives the loader's empty-line and comment filter, has its trailing newline removed, and is passed unchanged to `ndpi_handle_rule` for protocol-rule parsing.

The admitted rule is split at its last `@`. The prefix before `@` remains the comma-separated attribute list, while `proto` becomes the attacker-controlled protocol suffix whose lookup decides whether a new custom protocol must be created.

The protocol suffix from step 3 is not recognized, so lookup returns `NDPI_PROTOCOL_UNKNOWN` and leaves `def == NULL`. That control state selects the new custom-protocol creation branch instead of reusing an existing default slot.

For an unknown protocol, `ndpi_handle_rule` derives the new slot index from the current supported-protocol count. This value is then used as the target `protoId` in `ndpi_set_proto_defaults`; the later failed-growth path and ASan's read past the old heap region show that, on the crashing iteration, this derived `proto_id` is at the old allocation limit.
Because the derived `protoId` from step 5 is already at the current table boundary, `ndpi_set_proto_defaults` enters the growth path and asks `ndpi_realloc` for a larger `proto_defaults` array.

The witnessed run takes the allocation-failure branch: `ndpi_realloc` returns `NULL`, so `ndpi_set_proto_defaults` exits immediately without updating either `ndpi_str->proto_defaults` or `ndpi_str->proto_defaults_num_allocated`.

Root cause. After the failed growth in step 7, the caller still indexes `proto_defaults` with the boundary `proto_id` from step 5. Since the array and allocation count were left unchanged, this creates an out-of-bounds `def` pointer into redzone memory past the old heap array.
Later in the same admitted rule, the parser encounters a `tcp:` element. This marks the rule for default-port insertion and prepares `value` for the port-processing branch that dereferences `def`.

Sink. The `tcp:` branch walks `def->tcp_default_ports`, but step 8 already made `def` point beyond the unchanged heap array. Reading `port_low` performs the 2-byte heap-buffer-overflow reported by AddressSanitizer.

cross_validation.root_cause_matches_allocation_context: Yes. ASan names the original 512-entry `proto_defaults` allocation created by `ndpi_set_proto_defaults` during initialization; the fine trace explains the later unchecked-growth failure that makes `ndpi_handle_rule` index exactly past that same heap object.

format.name: newline-delimited nDPI protocols rules file
format.contract: The staged witness is an in-memory text file consumed by `load_protocols_file_fd`. The crashing path requires an admitted rule with an `@<unknown protocol>` suffix and a later `tcp:` element so `ndpi_handle_rule` takes the custom-protocol path, derives `proto_id = ndpi_str->num_supported_protocols`, and then processes TCP default ports through `def`. Under the harness's size-seeded allocation-failure schedule, the `ndpi_set_proto_defaults` growth attempt for that rule fails, leaves `proto_defaults` unchanged, and the later `tcp:` handling dereferences the unchecked `def = &ndpi_str->proto_defaults[proto_id]` alias; the saved ASan report shows that alias resolves just past the old heap allocation.
